reader.title: Killing of Jasper Vance
bases: Two deputy constables shot the man while trying to arrest his wife; no crowd or mob is reported (A2, A3, A4, A5).
The three December 11 reports are the same Rock Island dispatch (A2, A3, A4) and the Watertown brief reads as a condensed rewrite of it (A5); no independent or local account was found.

summary.text: The killing of Jasper Vance was the fatal shooting of a Black man by two deputy constables in the countryside near Rock Island, Arkansas, in December 1880, as they tried to arrest his wife.
According to a wire dispatch, he swore they would take her only over his dead body and was shot in the fight that followed.
The story ran as a short item in Chicago, Wheeling, Omaha and Watertown, Wisconsin, under headlines that cast him as a husband who died defending his wife.

A dispatch dated Rock Island, December 10, reported that Deputy Constables Henry and Solomon Reddick had gone into the country the previous night to arrest the wife of a man it described as "a negro."
The Chicago Tribune put the distance at four miles, while the Wheeling and Omaha versions said nine.
The dispatch gave no reason for the arrest and did not name the wife.
When the deputies arrived, the husband "swore they could take his wife only over his dead body," and, in the dispatch's words, "a fight ensued" in which the constables shot and mortally wounded him.
A weekly news summary in the Watertown Republican said that he "defended his house" and was shot dead before his wife's arrest was carried out, placing the shooting on December 10.
The only account of the fight is the dispatch, which does not say who began it or whether anyone besides the constables saw it.
No report of an inquest, an arrest of the constables or any later proceeding was found in the coverage, which also does not say what became of the wife.
Northern papers printed the Rock Island dispatch on December 11 nearly word for word but under different headings.
The Chicago Tribune titled it "Died for His Wife" among a column of crime briefs, and the Wheeling Daily Intelligencer used "Negro Killed by Constables."
The Omaha Daily Bee headed it "Defending His Wife" and billed it in its front-page deck as "A Determined Darkey Dies in Defense of His Wife in Arkansas."
Four days later the Watertown Republican reduced it to one sentence identifying the victim as "Joseph Vance (colored)."
None of the papers commented on the shooting, and none questioned the constables' conduct or gave the man's side beyond his reported vow.
The victim's name varies by paper: Jasper Vance in Chicago, Jasper Nance in Wheeling, Joseph Nance in Omaha and Joseph Vance in Watertown.
The dispatch's "last night" points to December 9, while the Watertown summary gives December 10, possibly the dispatch's own date.
The dispatch bodies said he was mortally wounded, though their headlines said he died, and Watertown said he was shot dead.

accounts.label: Rock Island wire dispatch
accounts.gist: The deputies went into the country at night to arrest Vance's wife; he swore they could take her only over his dead body, a fight followed, and the constables shot and mortally wounded him.

accounts.label: Weekly news summary
accounts.gist: Two constables tried to arrest the wife of Joseph Vance on the 10th; he defended his house and was shot dead before the arrest was made.

framing.detail: Chicago headed the dispatch 'Died for His Wife' and printed it without comment among other crime briefs.
Wheeling headed it 'Negro Killed by Constables'.
Omaha headed it 'Defending His Wife' and billed it in its deck as 'A Determined Darkey Dies in Defense of His Wife in Arkansas'.
Watertown condensed it to one sentence identifying the victim as '(colored)' among other crime notes.

conflicts.note: Transmission or typesetting variants of one dispatch; no version has better standing.
The December 10 dispatch's 'last night' is closer to the source than the weekly summary's date, which may be the dispatch date.
Headlines of A2-A4 say he died or was killed; bodies say mortally wounded.
